newsitem.title: USA: World Wide Web addresses on ads - Who needs 'em?.
newsitem.headline: World Wide Web addresses on ads - Who needs 'em?.

text.p: World Wide Web addresses have become the ubiquitous signature of most print and TV advertising.

While the omnipresent "www.company.com" appearing at the bottom of TV screens, and magazine and newspaper ads may be interesting information, it is relevant to only one in five adults, says J. Walker Smith, managing partner of Yankelovich Partners.

Marketers may have overlooked this in rush to get on the Web, said Smith, whose firm Monday releases its Cybercitizen Report II, the second annual Yankelovitch report on the behaviour of cyberspace users.

"Only 21.5 percent of all adults have any potential interest in a Web address in cyberspace," Smith said. Those who are so inclined tend to be mostly male, upscale baby boomers, although more women are plugging in, Smith said.
Of those currently using the Internet, 35 percent are under age 30, 49 percent are aged 30 to 39, and only 16 percent are age 50 and older, the report found.
Relevance notwithstanding, advertisers are posting their Web addresses on everything from business cards to billboards.
"It's novel. It's exciting. It's new," Smith explained. "There is a faddish curiosity about it. Marketers feel they need it."

One of them, Rishad Tobaccowala, president of Giant Step, an interactive media subsidiary of Leo Burnett Co., cites two reasons for the rash of Web addresses in advertising, "There's no incremental cost to putting the address in the ad. And it also says how cool and with it they are."

Web sites vary widely in their objectives, Tobaccowala said. Some companies use Web sites for marketing communications, some just for customer service, some for employee information or public relations.
"The key is, everyone is doing it early because they think it's an additional frontier," Tobaccowala said.
Recent studies have projected World Wide Web ad revenue in the year 2000 to jump to somewhere between $2 billion to $5 billion, up from the $200 million to $300 million range this year.
In terms of product categories, however, Yankelovich's Smith said he has seen no change in opportunities over the past 18 months.
"Things that sell most on the Internet are the things you'd expect: computer software, travel, tickets and reservations, and clothing," Smith said.

Currently, Web advertising makes the most sense for products and services that are heavily dependent on information, Smith said. He sees growth potential in information-heavy categories such as pharmaceuticals and automotive, as well as items that can be sampled on the Web, such as music, software and videos.

Not every marketer needs to have a Web site, and certainly not every brand, Tobaccowala said. He recommended, however, that major marketers do some dabbling in cybermarketing in order to be positioned for the coming explosion in the medium.
He warned advertisers not to expect too much from these early attempts.
"You're more likely to learn what doesn't work and how to fix it than to nail it the first time out," he said.
